The build takes under a second and yields 6,853,781 pairs, exactly one per SCV: every SCV is cited by exactly one VCV level statement. Keep vcv_statement_id, not just the accession; its suffix is what tells a -CP submission from a -NOCP or -EP one. Swap vcv for rcv to map SCVs to RCV accessions.

A useful identity: a VCV accession's number is the variation id. VCV000000010 is clinvar:10, with no exceptions across all 9 million VCV propositions.

items.title: Joins that lie
items.text:
Every one of these returns a plausible answer with no error. Check them first when a count looks low.

Columns that point at more than one table

Column Points at Dispatch on object_id on every proposition table condition, conditionSet, therapy or therapyGroup object_type variation.members[] allele, copyNumberCount, or copyNumberChange ga4gh:VA. / ga4gh:CN. / ga4gh:CX. vcv_evidenceLine.evidence_items[], rcv_evidenceLine.evidence_items[] an SCV, or another statement in the same table clinvar.submission: vs VCV/RCV

Join every branch, or at least count the rows that matched nothing.

Releases before 1.1.0 stored pointers, not ids

In releases before 1.1.0, vartherapy-proposition.object_therapy (now propositionSomaticClinicalImpact.object_id) held a JSON-quoted pointer ("#/therapy/clinvar.therapy:…"), and each variant gene-list entry held a #/gene/ncbigene:… pointer. Both now hold bare ids, and the 1.1.0 backfill rewrote the published Parquet for past releases. Parquet downloaded before the backfill still has the old tables and the old form. These expressions return the bare id from either form:

regexp_replace(trim(p.object_therapy, '"'), '^#/[A-Za-z]+/', '')   -- -> clinvar.therapy:…
replace(g.gene, '#/gene/', '')                                      -- -> ncbigene:…

The gene context is not the variant's genes

gene_context_name is a gene symbol, and symbols are not unique (BTBD8 names two NCBI genes), so join on gene_context_id, its ncbigene: id (from 1.1.0). Both are filled in only on SCV propositions (6,815,040 of them) and are NULL on every VCV and RCV proposition, so filtering aggregates by them returns nothing. Both name one representative gene per variant, chosen upstream, not the genes the submitter named (those are in submitted_gene_symbols); see Gene context. To find a gene's variants, use the variant's gene list, which carries ncbigene: ids, as in the PubMed-ids-for-a-gene recipe.

Next: Recipes puts these joins to work on real questions.

items.title: Beyond DuckDB
items.text:
Release

Outputs and timings on this page are from the 2026-10 monthly release (published 14 Oct 2026), run on a laptop against downloaded files with pyarrow 26, pandas 3, polars 2 and DuckDB 1.5.

Parquet is an open format, so any tool that reads it can read these files. This page does the same small task in each, so you can compare them: count the expert-panel SCVs by normalized classification, reading only the two fields that needs.

The expected answer, whichever tool you use:

code                    n
pathogenic              9,906
uncertain significance  3,954
likely pathogenic       2,940
likely benign           2,822
benign                  2,807
…

Whatever the tool, the rule from Anatomy of a Table holds: read only the columns you need. scv.parquet is 3.2 GB on disk and about 21 GB once loaded whole (2026-10-18 release).

items.title: DuckDB from Python
items.text:
The SQL on the rest of this track runs unchanged from Python, and .df() hands the result to pandas:

import duckdb

df = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT classification.primaryCoding.code AS code, count(*) AS n
    FROM 'scv.parquet'
    WHERE quality.name = 'expert panel'
    GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC
""").df()
print(df.head())

Use this when the work is mostly joins and filtering: DuckDB does them out of memory, and only the small result becomes a DataFrame.

items.title: pyarrow
items.text:
pyarrow reads the schema and metadata from the footer, and can read individual fields out of nested columns:

import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import pyarrow.compute as pc

pf = pq.ParquetFile("scv.parquet")                     # opening reads only the footer
print(pf.metadata.num_rows, "rows in", pf.metadata.num_row_groups, "row groups")
print(pf.schema_arrow.field("quality").type)

# Read two nested fields, not the whole table; they come back as columns "code" and "name"
t = pq.read_table("scv.parquet",
                  columns=["classification.primaryCoding.code", "quality.name"])
ep = t.filter(pc.equal(t["name"], "expert panel"))
print(ep.group_by("code").aggregate([("code", "count")])
        .sort_by([("code_count", "descending")]).slice(0, 5).to_pylist())

A dotted path in columns= reads just that leaf. Note that the result names the column by its last segment (code, name), not the full path.

items.title: pandas
items.text:
pandas reads Parquet through pyarrow, with the same columns=:

import pandas as pd

# columns= is essential: without it pandas loads every column, about 21 GB for scv
df = pd.read_parquet("scv.parquet",
                     columns=["classification.primaryCoding.code", "quality.name"])
print(df.columns.tolist())                               # ['code', 'name']
print(df.loc[df["name"] == "expert panel", "code"].value_counts().head())

Never pd.read_parquet a big table without columns=

It loads every column, including the multi-GB data column, into memory. On scv.parquet that is about 21 GB. The process is killed or the machine swaps.

items.title: polars
items.text:
polars' scan_parquet is lazy: it builds a query plan and, on .collect(), reads only the columns and rows the plan needs:

import polars as pl

out = (
    pl.scan_parquet("scv.parquet")                       # lazy: nothing is read yet
      .select(code=pl.col("classification").struct.field("primaryCoding").struct.field("code"),
              level=pl.col("quality").struct.field("name"))
      .filter(pl.col("level") == "expert panel")
      .group_by("code").len()
      .sort("len", descending=True)
      .collect()                                         # reads only the needed columns
)
print(out.head())

Use scan_parquet, not read_parquet: the eager read_parquet loads the file first, with the same memory problem as pandas.

items.title: R
items.text:
The arrow package opens a file as a dataset and translates dplyr verbs into a column-pruned scan; nothing is read until collect():

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

open_dataset("scv.parquet") |>
  transmute(code  = classification$primaryCoding$code,
            level = quality$name) |>
  filter(level == "expert panel") |>
  count(code, sort = TRUE) |>
  collect()

The duckdb R package is the other route: it runs the SQL from this track unchanged.

items.title: Spark and cloud warehouses
items.text:
The files load directly into Spark (spark.read.parquet(...)) and into cloud warehouses: as BigQuery external or loaded tables from a Cloud Storage copy, or as Athena tables over an S3 copy. Copy the files into your own bucket first; data.clinvar-gkm.org is a download host, not a query endpoint for warehouse engines.

What survives the trip:

  • STRUCT and LIST columns arrive as the engine's record and array types (STRUCT/ARRAY in BigQuery and Spark, struct/array in Athena), so dotted access like classification.name works the same way.
  • data is a string everywhere. Parse it with the engine's JSON functions (JSON_VALUE in BigQuery, get_json_object in Spark) only when a field has no typed column.
  • Ids are plain strings. The joins on Joining Tables translate directly, prefix dispatch included.

items.title: Spreadsheets and GUI tools
items.text:
Excel, Google Sheets and most GUI tools can't open Parquet, and even those that can shouldn't open a multi-GB table. Filter to the rows you need first, then export that slice to CSV:

duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT id, name FROM 'condition.parquet') TO 'conditions.csv' (HEADER)"

Recipes → Export a slice has a fuller example. With no terminal at all, the DuckDB Web Shell can open a small downloaded file in the browser and export the result.

items.title: Which tool when
items.text: For exploring and for joins, DuckDB, from the command line or from Python or R: it reads only what a query needs and handles joins larger than memory. For a dataframe workflow in Python, polars with scan_parquet gives the same column pruning with a dataframe API. Use pandas or pyarrow when a library you depend on expects their objects, and always pass columns=. Reach for Spark or a warehouse only when the data has to live next to other large data in your cloud. For everyone else, a few GB of Parquet on a laptop is small.

items.title: Working at Scale
items.text:
Release

Timings and measured results on this page are from the 2026-10 monthly release (published 14 Oct 2026), measured with DuckDB 1.5 on a laptop. File and column sizes are from the 2026-10-18 release. Your numbers will differ with the release and your machine.

Nine tables are over 500 MB: variation (3.9 GB), scv (3.2 GB), propositionPathogenicity (1.5 GB), allele (1.1 GB), location, and the RCV and VCV statements and evidence lines (0.5–0.9 GB each). The other thirteen are each about 11 MB or less. A handful of habits keeps queries over the big ones fast on a laptop.

items.title: Name your columns
items.text:
Parquet stores each column separately, and a query reads only the columns it names. This is the single biggest lever you have. In scv.parquet the data column is 2.1 GB of the 3.2 GB on disk and 15.7 GB of the 21 GB in memory (the breakdown). A query that leaves it out reads a quarter of the file; one that names two small fields reads almost none of it.

To see where any table's bytes are, ask its metadata. This reads only the file footer:

SELECT split_part(path_in_schema, ',', 1)          AS col,
       round(sum(total_compressed_size)   / 1e9, 2) AS gb_on_disk,
       round(sum(total_uncompressed_size) / 1e9, 2) AS gb_in_memory
FROM parquet_metadata('scv.parquet')
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY gb_in_memory DESC;

The same holds for fields inside a STRUCT: classification.name reads that one field, not the whole classification record. Selecting * or the struct as a whole reads everything.

items.title: Reach into nested lists without unnest
items.text:
Several columns are lists of records: variation.extensions, variation.members, scv.contributions, scv.reportedIn. To filter on something inside them, prefer a list comprehension, [x.field FOR x IN list IF …], over unnest. unnest turns every list element into its own row before filtering; a comprehension filters each list in place.

The difference is large. Finding the variants in one gene by filtering variation.extensions takes 4 s and 1.5 GB as a comprehension and 37 s and 2.5 GB with unnest, for the same 5,942 variants. The gene rollup recipe shows the comprehension.

Use comprehensions rather than lambda functions (list_filter(l, x -> …)). DuckDB 1.5 deprecates that arrow syntax, and the replacement (lambda x: …) is too new for the browser console's engine. Comprehensions work in both.

items.title: Join on a plain equality
items.text: DuckDB joins two big tables fast, with a hash join, when the ON clause is one equality between them. Add a second condition (ON p.object_type = 'condition' AND c.id = p.object_id), or join through a function (ON list_contains(v.members, a.id)), and DuckDB 1.5 plans a nested-loop join instead, which compares row against row and runs for over an hour on propositionPathogenicity. Fold the extra condition into the key, ON c.id = CASE WHEN p.object_type = 'condition' THEN p.object_id END, or unnest the list in a subquery and join on the plain column. Seam B shows the first; Find the variant shows the second. Put EXPLAIN in front of a query to check before you run it: HASH_JOIN is the fast kind; NESTED_LOOP_JOIN, BLOCKWISE_NL_JOIN and PIECEWISE_MERGE_JOIN are the slow kinds.

items.title: Local or remote
items.text:
DuckDB reads Parquet over HTTPS with range requests: it fetches the file's footer first, then only the byte ranges of the row groups and columns a query needs. That makes some remote queries as cheap as local ones and others impossible:

Over the network Requests Works? DESCRIBE, count(*), parquet_metadata(…) footer only yes, in under a second on any table LIMIT n without a filter footer + first row group yes Any query on a small table (condition, gene, submitter, therapy, …) a few yes A filter, GROUP BY or join over a big table one per row group per column; 55 row groups in scv, about 223 in propositionPathogenicity slowly: 10–35 s per query, reading hundreds of MB; download for repeated or heavier work

The published files are not sorted by any lookup key, so even a filter for a single variant or SCV has to read every row group of the filtered column. The CDN in front of data.clinvar-gkm.org allows 250 requests per 10 seconds per client IP and blocks for 10 seconds past that (HTTP 429). From the command line, single-table scans and two-table joins on the big tables now complete within it (a GROUP BY over all of scv in about 30 s; a variant's PubMed ids in about 25 s), but each reads hundreds of megabytes, so repeated or larger work belongs on a downloaded copy.

The rule: query remotely to explore, download to analyze. Download the tables a question needs once (see Start Here), and every query on this page and in Recipes runs in seconds.

items.title: DuckDB settings for a laptop
items.text:
DuckDB's defaults suit most queries here: it uses every CPU core, caps itself at 80 % of RAM, and spills to a .tmp directory when a query needs more. When a big join or GROUP BY runs out of memory, you see this:

Out of Memory Error: could not allocate block of size 256.0 KiB (953.5 MiB/953.6 MiB used)

Possible solutions:
* Reducing the number of threads (SET threads=X)
* Disabling insertion-order preservation (SET preserve_insertion_order=false)
* Increasing the memory limit (SET memory_limit='...GB')

The suggestions are the right ones, in that order:

Setting Effect SET threads = 2; Each thread holds its own working memory; fewer threads means a smaller peak. SET preserve_insertion_order = false; Lets DuckDB skip buffering rows to keep them in file order. Use it whenever the result has an ORDER BY or order doesn't matter. SET memory_limit = '8GB'; Raises (or lowers) the cap. SET temp_directory = '/path/with/space'; Moves the spill files to a disk with room.

A GROUP BY on scv.description, a free-text column with millions of distinct values, fails as above with a 1 GB memory limit. With threads = 2 and preserve_insertion_order = false added, it finishes in under 3 seconds within the same limit.

For work you repeat, open a database file (duckdb clinvar-gkm.duckdb) rather than an in-memory session. Tables you create there persist, which is what makes the next section possible.

items.title: Materialize the joins you repeat
items.text:
Statements and propositions live in separate tables. An SCV row holds its classification but not the variant or condition it is about. Those are on the proposition, in one of four tables, each spelling the columns slightly differently. So any question about statements by subject (a variant), object (a condition, tumor type or therapy) or qualifier (gene context, mode of inheritance, penetrance) has to join two multi-GB tables first.

Paying for that join on every query is slow locally, and slower over the network: scv.parquet has no variant column, so a lookup for one variant must read every row group of the file. From the command line that takes about 25 seconds and hundreds of megabytes per query; in the browser's live console it can also exhaust memory or trip the CDN's rate limit (HTTP 429).

The fix is to run the join once, store the result as a table sorted by the column you look up most, and query that table instead. DuckDB has no CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW; CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT in a database file does the same job. You refresh it by re-running the script when you download a new release.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Download the four proposition tables and scv.parquet (see Start Here), then run this in the same directory. It writes a database file, clinvar-gkm.duckdb, that persists between sessions:

duckdb clinvar-gkm.duckdb < materialize.sql

-- materialize.sql
SET preserve_insertion_order = false;   -- lets DuckDB build large tables with less memory

-- 1. One proposition table: the four tables share one column schema, so one glob reads them all.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE prop AS
SELECT id, type AS proposition_type, predicate,
       subject_variant_id AS variant_id, object_id, object_type,
       gene_context_name, gene_context_id, mode_of_inheritance, penetrance, condition_qualifier_id
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet');

-- 2. SCV statements with their proposition's subject, object and qualifiers inlined,
--    sorted by variant so a lookup by variant touches one small slice of the table.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE scv_by_variant AS
SELECT p.variant_id, p.object_id, p.object_type, p.proposition_type, p.predicate,
       p.gene_context_name, p.gene_context_id, p.mode_of_inheritance, p.penetrance, p.condition_qualifier_id,
       s.id                     AS scv_id,
       s.classification.name    AS classification,
       s.quality.name           AS submission_level,
       s.direction,
       [c.contributor FOR c IN s.contributions IF c.activityType = 'submitted'][1] AS submitter_id,
       [r.pmid FOR r IN s.reportedIn IF r.pmid IS NOT NULL]                        AS pmids
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
ORDER BY p.variant_id, s.id;

The build takes about 30 seconds and peaks near 5 GB of memory. Every one of the 6,735,011 SCVs finds its proposition, and the database file comes to about 650 MB. Only the columns the questions below need are carried over. Add others, such as s.description or s.specifiedBy.name, the same way.

items.title: Query it
items.text:
Each of these returns in about 10 ms, where the same question against the raw Parquet files means a multi-GB join.

By subject (a variant)

-- PubMed ids cited by the SCVs for one variant
SELECT pmid, count(*) AS n_scvs,
       string_agg(replace(scv_id, 'clinvar.submission:', ''), ', ') AS cited_by
FROM (SELECT scv_id, unnest(pmids) AS pmid
      FROM scv_by_variant WHERE variant_id = 'clinvar:10')
GROUP BY pmid
ORDER BY n_scvs DESC, pmid;

By object (a condition)

-- What submitters have called variants for one condition
SELECT classification, count(*) AS n
FROM scv_by_variant
WHERE object_id = 'clinvar.trait:9580'      -- Hereditary spastic paraplegia 48
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC;

This matches propositions whose object is that condition. A proposition about a condition set that contains it has a clinvar.traitset: or clinvar.conditionset: object instead. To include those, expand the sets as shown in Joining Tables.

By qualifier

-- Pathogenic calls made under autosomal recessive inheritance, by submission level
SELECT submission_level, count(*) AS n
FROM scv_by_variant
WHERE mode_of_inheritance = 'Autosomal recessive inheritance'
  AND classification = 'Pathogenic'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC;

items.title: The same pattern for the aggregates
items.text:
VCV and RCV statements join to the same prop table. Add this to materialize.sql to get every aggregate statement for a variant in one lookup:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE vcv_by_variant AS
SELECT p.variant_id, p.object_id, p.proposition_type,
       v.id AS vcv_id, v.classification.name AS classification,
       v.quality.name AS aggregate_level, v.direction
FROM 'vcv.parquet' v
JOIN prop p ON p.id = v.proposition_id
ORDER BY p.variant_id, v.id;

It builds in about 6 seconds and holds all 9,079,449 VCV statements. For rcv, swap in rcv.parquet.

items.title: Share it as a sorted Parquet file
items.text:
A materialized table can go back out as Parquet. Because the rows are sorted by variant_id, DuckDB's per-row-group min/max statistics let a reader skip almost all of the file:

COPY scv_by_variant TO 'scv_by_variant.parquet' (FORMAT parquet);

The result is about 107 MB, versus 3.2 GB for scv.parquet. A WHERE variant_id = 'clinvar:10' lookup reads 1 of its 55 row groups. The same layout is what would make per-variant queries practical over the network, where every row group read is a request.

items.title: Errors that look worse than they are
items.text:
Parser Error: syntax error at or near "name": a column alias without AS. Many words used as column names in these tables are reserved in SQL, so SELECT value->>'name' name fails while SELECT value->>'name' AS name works. The same goes for type, data, key, value, rows, names, target, role, end and year. Always write AS.

Conversion Error: … can't be cast to the destination type STRUCT(…): comparing a STRUCT column to text, as in WHERE classification = 'Pathogenic'. Name the field: classification.name. See Reading a STRUCT column.

Text that prints : the DuckDB command line shows a newline inside a value as , so a list joined with newlines looks broken:

│ GM1 gangliosidosis
Mucopolysaccharidosis, MPS-IV-B │

The data is fine. Switch to .mode line to see the value as written, or join with '; ' instead.

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests: a remote query read too many row groups; see Local or remote.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
Release

Outputs, timings and memory figures on this page are from the 2026-10 monthly release (published 14 Oct 2026), run with DuckDB 1.5 on a laptop against downloaded files. Re-run a recipe to get today's numbers.

Each recipe answers one question: the question in plain language, a query you can run, and what to expect, including how long it takes and how much memory it uses. They run against downloaded files; each touches at least one multi-GB table, which is too much for the live console. See Start Here to download.

Change the line marked -- <- to ask about your own variant, condition, gene or submitter. Joining Tables explains each join used here.

Recipe Time Peak memory Everything ClinVar says about one variant < 1 s 0.6 GB PubMed ids cited for a variant < 1 s 0.4 GB Variants submitted for a condition < 1 s 1.1 GB One submitter's footprint < 1 s 0.1 GB Why a variant is "conflicting" < 1 s 0.3 GB Variants in a genomic window < 1 s 0.7 GB Gene rollup of ClinVar's calls 5 s 1.6 GB PubMed ids cited for every variant in a gene 5 s 1.5 GB Export a slice to CSV or Parquet < 1 s 0.4 GB

items.title: Everything ClinVar says about one variant
Find the variant
items.text:
If you know the ClinVar variation id, you already have it: clinvar:<id>. Otherwise look it up by any HGVS expression ClinVar lists for it (coding c., genomic g., non-coding n., on any transcript or assembly):

SELECT id, name
FROM 'variation.parquet'
WHERE list_contains(
        flatten([[h.nucleotideExpression.value FOR h IN e.value_hgvs_array] FOR e IN extensions]),
        'NM_000059.4:c.4090A>C');                                            -- <- your HGVS

id             name
clinvar:51592  NM_000059.4(BRCA2):c.4090A>C (p.Ile1364Leu)

This scans every variant's HGVS list: about 4.5 s and 1.4 GB. For a GRCh38 genomic expression, the allele table is much faster (0.2 s):

SELECT v.id, v.name
FROM 'allele.parquet' a
JOIN (SELECT id, name, unnest(members) AS member FROM 'variation.parquet') v
     ON v.member = a.id                   -- an equality join; list_contains() in ON plans a nested loop
WHERE a.name = 'NC_000013.11:g.32338445A>C';

items.title: ClinVar's aggregate calls
items.text:
One row for each VCV root statement (one per classification type) and each RCV (one per condition), with the condition names resolved:

WITH prop AS (                    -- all four proposition tables: one shared schema, one glob
  SELECT id, type, subject_variant_id AS variant_id, object_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
),
set_names AS (
  SELECT cs.id, string_agg(c.name, '; ' ORDER BY c.name) AS member_names
  FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(cid)
  JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = cid
  GROUP BY cs.id
),
agg AS (
  SELECT 'VCV' AS tier, id, proposition_id, quality.name AS level, classification.name AS classification FROM 'vcv.parquet'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'RCV', id, proposition_id, quality.name, classification.name FROM 'rcv.parquet'
)
SELECT a.tier, a.id AS statement, p.type AS proposition_type, a.level, a.classification,
       coalesce(c.name, sn.member_names) AS condition
FROM agg a
JOIN prop p ON p.id = a.proposition_id
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = p.object_id
LEFT JOIN set_names sn ON sn.id = p.object_id
WHERE p.variant_id = 'clinvar:51592'                                         -- <- your variant
  AND NOT regexp_matches(a.id, '-(PG|EP|CP|NOCP|NOCL|FLAG)(-T[0-9])?$')     -- root statements only
ORDER BY a.tier DESC, a.id;

tier  statement                proposition_type                 level              classification        condition
VCV   VCV000051592.122-G-NP    ClinvarNotProvidedProposition    no classification  not provided          not specified
VCV   VCV000051592.122-G-PATH  VariantPathogenicityProposition  expert panel       Benign                Breast-ovarian cancer, familial, susceptibility to, 2
RCV   RCV000044344.34-G-PATH   VariantPathogenicityProposition  criteria provided  Benign                Hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome
RCV   RCV000113272.28-G-PATH   VariantPathogenicityProposition  expert panel       Benign                Breast-ovarian cancer, familial, susceptibility to, 2
…

Drop the root-statement filter to see each level statement as well (-EP, -CP, -NOCP, …); Reading a variant's statements explains them.

items.title: Every submission
items.text:
Who submitted, what they said, at what level, for which condition, and when they last evaluated it:

WITH prop AS (                    -- all four proposition tables: one shared schema, one glob
  SELECT id, type, subject_variant_id AS variant_id, object_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
),
set_names AS (
  SELECT cs.id, string_agg(c.name, '; ' ORDER BY c.name) AS member_names
  FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(cid)
  JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = cid
  GROUP BY cs.id
)
SELECT replace(s.id, 'clinvar.submission:', '') AS scv,
       sub.name                AS submitter,
       s.classification.name   AS classification,
       s.quality.name          AS level,
       coalesce(c.name, sn.member_names) AS condition,
       [x.date FOR x IN s.contributions IF x.activityType = 'evaluated'][1] AS last_evaluated
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
LEFT JOIN 'submitter.parquet' sub
       ON sub.id = [x.contributor FOR x IN s.contributions IF x.activityType = 'submitted'][1]
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = p.object_id
LEFT JOIN set_names sn ON sn.id = p.object_id
WHERE p.variant_id = 'clinvar:51592'                                         -- <- your variant
ORDER BY last_evaluated DESC;

scv              submitter                                              classification  level              condition                                  last_evaluated
SCV000072357.18  Labcorp Genetics (formerly Invitae), Labcorp           Benign          criteria provided  Hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome  2026-02-03
SCV000602753.7   ARUP Laboratories, Molecular Genetics and Genomics, …  Benign          criteria provided  not provided                               2025-05-19
SCV004243027.2   Center for Genomic Medicine, Rigshospitalet, …         Benign          criteria provided  not specified                              2025-03-04
…

36 submissions for this variant. Each of these two queries takes under a second.

items.title: PubMed ids cited for a variant
items.text:
PubMed ids appear only on SCVs (individual submissions), in scv.reportedIn[].pmid. The variant, VCV and RCV records carry none. So the query goes from the variant to its propositions, and from the propositions to the SCVs that cite them.

WITH v AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM 'variation.parquet' WHERE id = 'clinvar:10'         -- <- your variant
),
prop AS (                                     -- all four proposition tables, one glob
  SELECT id, subject_variant_id AS variant_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
),
cites AS (                                    -- one row per (SCV, cited PubMed id)
  SELECT p.variant_id, s.id AS scv_id, unnest(s.reportedIn).pmid AS pmid
  FROM 'scv.parquet' s
  JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
  WHERE p.variant_id IN (SELECT id FROM v)
)
SELECT v.id AS variant_id, v.name AS variant_name, c.pmid,
       'https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/' || c.pmid AS pubmed_url,
       count(DISTINCT c.scv_id) AS n_scvs,
       string_agg(DISTINCT replace(c.scv_id, 'clinvar.submission:', ''), ', '
                  ORDER BY replace(c.scv_id, 'clinvar.submission:', '')) AS scvs
FROM cites c JOIN v ON v.id = c.variant_id
WHERE c.pmid IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY n_scvs DESC, c.pmid;

For clinvar:10, NM_000410.4(HFE):c.187C>G (p.His63Asp), the most-cited PubMed ids, each with the SCVs that cite it. Selected columns:

pmid      n_scvs  scvs
19159930  5       SCV000198337.5, SCV001194094.2, SCV001251532.1, SCV001519563.1, SCV002568070.8
8696333   5       SCV000461883.3, SCV001519563.1, SCV002502480.1, SCV002506442.3, SCV006582525.2
19554541  4       SCV000198337.5, SCV000461883.3, SCV001194094.2, SCV002769510.1
…

The query leaves out one kind of citation on purpose: scv.specifiedBy.reportedIn.pmid is the paper describing the submitter's classification method, such as the ACMG/AMP guidelines (PMID 25741868). It appears on most submissions, so it says nothing about the variant. Add it only if you want it.

Asking this often?

If you look up many variants, materialize the statement–proposition join once. Each lookup then takes about 10 ms, and the PubMed ids are already gathered into a list per SCV.

items.title: Variants submitted for a condition
items.text:
Every variant with a submission for one condition, with how submitters classified it. A submission can name the condition directly or as a member of a condition set, so the query collects both (see Seam B):

WITH target AS (
  SELECT id FROM 'condition.parquet' WHERE name = 'Marfan syndrome'          -- <- your condition
),
members AS (                      -- one row per (condition set, member id)
  SELECT cs.id AS set_id, cid AS member_id
  FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(cid)
),
sets AS (                         -- the sets that list the condition directly
  SELECT m.set_id AS id FROM members m JOIN target ON target.id = m.member_id
),
objects AS (                      -- the condition itself, plus every set that contains it (one level of nesting)
  SELECT id FROM target
  UNION
  SELECT id FROM sets
  UNION
  SELECT m.set_id FROM members m JOIN sets ON sets.id = m.member_id
),
prop AS (
  SELECT id, subject_variant_id AS variant_id, object_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
)
SELECT p.variant_id, v.name AS variant_name,
       count(*) AS scvs,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.classification.primaryCoding.code IN ('pathogenic', 'likely pathogenic'))  AS p_lp,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.classification.primaryCoding.code = 'uncertain significance')           AS vus,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.classification.primaryCoding.code IN ('benign', 'likely benign'))       AS b_lb
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
JOIN 'variation.parquet' v ON v.id = p.variant_id
WHERE p.object_id IN (SELECT id FROM objects)
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY scvs DESC, p.variant_id
LIMIT 10;

variant_id      variant_name                                scvs  p_lp  vus  b_lb
clinvar:163462  NM_000138.5(FBN1):c.7754T>C (p.Ile2585Thr)  13    13    0    0
clinvar:16451   NM_000138.5(FBN1):c.3509G>A (p.Arg1170His)  13    1     4    7
clinvar:42394   NM_000138.5(FBN1):c.5788+5G>A               13    13    0    0
clinvar:16445   NM_000138.5(FBN1):c.8176C>T (p.Arg2726Trp)  11    0     4    7
…

The counts use the normalized classification.primaryCoding.code, not the submitted text; Anatomy of a Table explains why.

items.title: One submitter's footprint
items.text:
What one organization has submitted, by classification and submission level. The Auditing a Submitter's Footprint story walks through this kind of audit in depth.

WITH sub AS (
  SELECT id FROM 'submitter.parquet' WHERE name = 'Mayo Clinic Laboratories, Mayo Clinic'   -- <- your submitter
)
SELECT s.classification.primaryCoding.code AS classification,
       s.quality.name                      AS level,
       count(*)                            AS scvs
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
WHERE [c.contributor FOR c IN s.contributions IF c.activityType = 'submitted'][1] IN (SELECT id FROM sub)
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY scvs DESC;

classification          level                           scvs
uncertain significance  criteria provided               18,832
benign                  criteria provided               18,791
likely benign           criteria provided               10,983
pathogenic              criteria provided                2,543
likely pathogenic       criteria provided                2,047
…

Find a submitter's exact name with SELECT id, name FROM 'submitter.parquet' WHERE name ILIKE '%mayo%'.

items.title: Why a variant is "conflicting"
items.text:
ClinVar calls 178,208 variants Conflicting classifications of pathogenicity. This finds them:

SELECT classification.name AS classification, count(*) AS variants
FROM 'vcv.parquet'
WHERE regexp_matches(id, '-G-PATH$')                -- the germline pathogenicity root statement
  AND classification.name ILIKE 'conflicting%'
GROUP BY ALL;

To see why one variant is conflicting, list the submissions behind each level of its pathogenicity call, grouped by what they said. This walks the VCV evidence lines down to the SCVs (Seam E):

WITH scv_vcv AS (
  SELECT s.id AS vcv_statement_id, it AS scv_id
  FROM (SELECT id, unnest(has_evidence_lines) AS el_id FROM 'vcv.parquet'
        WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%-G-PATH-%') s                       -- <- your variant's VCV accession
  JOIN 'vcv_evidenceLine.parquet' el ON el.id = s.el_id,
       unnest(el.evidence_items) AS t(it)
  WHERE it LIKE 'clinvar.submission:%'
)
SELECT x.vcv_statement_id,
       s.classification.primaryCoding.code AS classification,
       count(*) AS scvs,
       string_agg(DISTINCT sub.name, '; ' ORDER BY sub.name) AS submitters
FROM scv_vcv x
JOIN 'scv.parquet' s ON s.id = x.scv_id
LEFT JOIN 'submitter.parquet' sub
       ON sub.id = [c.contributor FOR c IN s.contributions IF c.activityType = 'submitted'][1]
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY x.vcv_statement_id, scvs DESC, classification;

vcv_statement_id              classification              scvs  submitters
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-CP    pathogenic                  40    3billion; AiLife Diagnostics, …
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-CP    likely pathogenic            2    Genomic Medicine Center of Excellence, …
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-CP    uncertain significance       2    Cambridge Genomics Laboratory, …
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-CP    pathogenic, low penetrance   1    Labcorp Genetics (formerly Invitae), Labcorp
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-FLAG  benign                       1    Pathology and Clinical Laboratory Medicine, …
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-FLAG  uncertain significance       1    Laboratory for Molecular Medicine, …
VCV000000010.141-G-PATH-NOCP  pathogenic                   8    Clinical Genetics DNA and cytogenetics Diagnostics Lab, …

The call comes from the -CP level, the highest present. Among those 45 submissions, two say uncertain significance against 42 pathogenic or likely pathogenic; that disagreement is the conflict. The -NOCP and -FLAG submissions are listed but don't count toward the call. The VCV accession number is the variation id zero-padded to nine digits (clinvar:10 → VCV000000010).

items.title: Variants in a genomic window
items.text:
Every variant (alleles and copy-number variants) whose location overlaps a window on GRCh38 chromosome 13. Coordinates are interbase (0-based, end-exclusive), so the window [32338400, 32338500) covers 1-based positions 32,338,401–32,338,500.

WITH seq AS (
  SELECT id FROM 'sequenceReference.parquet' WHERE name = 'NC_000013.11'    -- <- chromosome (RefSeq accession)
),
loc AS (
  SELECT id, loc_start_min, loc_start_max, loc_end_min, loc_end_max FROM 'location.parquet'
  WHERE sequence_reference_id = (SELECT id FROM seq)
    AND loc_start_max < 32338500 AND loc_end_min > 32338400                 -- <- window
),
vrs AS (
  SELECT id, location_id FROM 'allele.parquet'
  UNION ALL SELECT id, location_id FROM 'copyNumberCount.parquet'
  UNION ALL SELECT id, location_id FROM 'copyNumberChange.parquet'
)
SELECT v.id, v.name, l.loc_start_min, l.loc_start_max, l.loc_end_min, l.loc_end_max
FROM vrs
JOIN loc l ON l.id = vrs.location_id
JOIN (SELECT id, name, unnest(members) AS member FROM 'variation.parquet') v ON v.member = vrs.id
ORDER BY l.loc_start_max, v.id;

id              name                                              loc_start_min  loc_start_max  loc_end_min  loc_end_max
clinvar:146305  GRCh38/hg38 13q11-34(chr13:18445862-114327173)x1  NULL           18445861       114327173    NULL
clinvar:151282  GRCh38/hg38 13q11-34(chr13:18456040-114340285)x3  NULL           18456039       114340285    NULL
clinvar:59851   GRCh38/hg38 13q11-34(chr13:18565048-114327173)x3  NULL           18565047       114327173    NULL
…

243 variants in this 100-base window. 35 of them are copy-number variants whose start or end is an uncertain range, like the three above: ClinVar knows the deleted or duplicated span covers at least [loc_start_max, loc_end_min), but not how far beyond it. For a definite coordinate the min and max columns are equal.

The query matches on the span each variant certainly covers. To include every variant that may reach the window, match on the outer bounds instead, treating NULL as unbounded: coalesce(loc_start_min, 0) < 32338500 AND coalesce(loc_end_max, 9e9) > 32338400 (638 variants here).

From release 1.1.0

The loc_start_min … loc_end_max columns exist in location.parquet from release 1.1.0. On earlier releases, filter on loc_start and loc_end instead (loc_start < 32338500 AND loc_end > 32338400); that finds 208 variants here, because it skips every location whose start or end is an uncertain range (their range is only in location.data).

items.title: Gene rollup of ClinVar's calls
items.text:
ClinVar's germline pathogenicity call for every variant in a gene. Genes come from the variant's ClinVar gene list (ncbigene: ids), not the free-text gene_context_name, which isn't a reliable gene join.

WITH v AS (                       -- variants whose ClinVar gene list names the gene
  SELECT x.id
  FROM (SELECT id,
               unnest(flatten([[replace(g.gene, '#/gene/', '') FOR g IN e.value_gene_array   -- bare ncbigene: id
                                IF g.relationship_type IN ('within single gene', 'within multiple genes by overlap',
                                                           'asserted, but not computed')]
                               FOR e IN extensions IF e.name = 'clinvarGeneList'])) AS gene_id
        FROM 'variation.parquet') x
  JOIN 'gene.parquet' gene ON gene.id = x.gene_id      -- an equality join, so DuckDB plans a fast hash join
  WHERE gene.name = 'MYH7'                                                    -- <- your gene symbol
)
SELECT classification.name AS clinvar_call, count(*) AS variants
FROM 'vcv.parquet'
WHERE regexp_matches(id, '-G-PATH$')                                          -- germline pathogenicity root
  AND 'clinvar:' || CAST(substr(id, 4, 9) AS INTEGER) IN (SELECT id FROM v)   -- VCV accession number = variation id
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY variants DESC;

clinvar_call                                  variants
Uncertain significance                        3,005
Likely benign                                 1,690
Conflicting classifications of pathogenicity    555
Likely pathogenic                               256
Benign                                          146
Pathogenic                                       96
…

About 5 s and 1.6 GB, nearly all of it reading the gene lists in the 4 GB variation.parquet. The relationship_type filter drops large copy-number variants that merely overlap the gene and variants near it; remove it to include them. The replace(…, '#/gene/', '') lets the query run on any release: before 1.1.0 each gene was a #/gene/ncbigene:… pointer, and on the bare ncbigene: ids from 1.1.0 on it changes nothing.

Reach into nested lists with [… FOR … IN …], not unnest

The gene filter above uses a list comprehension. Written instead with unnest(extensions) and unnest(value_gene_array), the same filter returns the same 5,942 variants but takes about 37 s and 2.5 GB, because unnest expands every variant's whole extension list into rows first.

items.title: PubMed ids cited for every variant in a gene
items.text:
The gene filter from the rollup, joined to the PubMed query:

WITH v AS (                                  -- variants whose ClinVar gene list names the gene
  SELECT x.id, x.name
  FROM (SELECT id, name,
               unnest(flatten([[replace(g.gene, '#/gene/', '') FOR g IN e.value_gene_array   -- bare ncbigene: id
                                -- drop large CNVs that merely overlap the gene, and near-gene variants:
                                IF g.relationship_type IN ('within single gene', 'within multiple genes by overlap',
                                                           'asserted, but not computed')]
                               FOR e IN extensions IF e.name = 'clinvarGeneList'])) AS gene_id
        FROM 'variation.parquet') x
  JOIN 'gene.parquet' gene ON gene.id = x.gene_id      -- an equality join, so DuckDB plans a fast hash join
  WHERE gene.name = 'MYH7'                                                     -- <- your gene symbol
),
prop AS (
  SELECT id, subject_variant_id AS variant_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
),
cites AS (
  SELECT p.variant_id, s.id AS scv_id, unnest(s.reportedIn).pmid AS pmid
  FROM 'scv.parquet' s
  JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
  WHERE p.variant_id IN (SELECT id FROM v)
)
SELECT v.id AS variant_id, v.name AS variant_name, c.pmid,
       count(DISTINCT c.scv_id) AS n_scvs
FROM cites c JOIN v ON v.id = c.variant_id
WHERE c.pmid IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY v.id, c.pmid;

One row per (variant, PubMed id). For MYH7 that is 6,976 rows covering 1,694 variants and 1,093 distinct PubMed ids, in about 5 s and 1.5 GB. For a list of distinct PubMed ids instead, wrap the final SELECT and group by pmid.

items.title: Export a slice to CSV or Parquet
items.text:
Spreadsheets and many tools can't read Parquet, and you rarely want a whole table anyway. Wrap any query in COPY to write its result to a file:

-- Expert-panel and practice-guideline submissions, with their variant
COPY (
  WITH prop AS (
    SELECT id, subject_variant_id AS variant_id FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
  )
  SELECT replace(s.id, 'clinvar.submission:', '') AS scv,
         p.variant_id,
         s.classification.name AS classification,
         s.quality.name        AS level
  FROM 'scv.parquet' s
  JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
  WHERE s.quality.name IN ('expert panel', 'practice guidelines')
) TO 'expert_scvs.csv' (HEADER);

That writes 25,379 rows plus a header. For another analytics tool, write Parquet instead, which keeps the column types and is far smaller: TO 'expert_scvs.parquet' (FORMAT parquet).

items.title: Anatomy of a Table
items.text:
Release

Outputs, sizes and counts on this page are from the 2026-10 monthly release (published 14 Oct 2026). They change with every release; re-run a query to get today's numbers.

One bundle section, one table

The JSON bundle is organized into 22 named sections (variation, scv, condition, …). The Parquet release turns each section into exactly one table, stored as one file (variation.parquet, scv.parquet, condition.parquet, …), with one row per object in that section. This track calls them tables.

All 22 tables are built the same way, so what you learn reading one applies to the rest. This page covers what they have in common: how to read a table's schema, the id and data columns, the column types and how to reach inside nested ones, and which columns to leave alone. The column reference then documents each table individually in that shared shape. Everything here stays inside one table at a time; no joins.

Every query here except the last runs in the live console. Paste it in and replace '<table>.parquet' with '{BASE}/<table>.parquet'. The last one scans a 3 GB table, so it belongs on your machine.

items.title: Read the schema first
items.text:
DESCRIBE lists a table's columns and types. It reads only the file's footer, so it is instant even on the largest table, locally or over the network.

DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM 'condition.parquet';

column_name    column_type
id             VARCHAR
type           VARCHAR
conceptType    VARCHAR
name           VARCHAR
aliases        VARCHAR[]
primaryCoding  STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[])
mappings       STRUCT(coding STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[]), relation VARCHAR)[]

The types you will meet:

Type What it holds How to read it VARCHAR, BIGINT A plain value Use the column directly VARCHAR[] A list of values aliases[1] (1-based), len(aliases), unnest(aliases) for one row per element STRUCT(...) A record with named fields primaryCoding.code STRUCT(...)[] A list of records unnest(mappings), then dot into each one

Run the same DESCRIBE on scv.parquet and most of its columns are STRUCTs: classification, strength, quality, specifiedBy, contributions, extensions. The full list for every table, with a description of each column, is in the column reference.

items.title: Every table has an id
items.text:
Every row has an id, and its shape tells you which table it belongs to (clinvar.trait:2645 is a condition, clinvar:51592 a variant; see Ids tell you where to look). Ids are how tables connect, and they are how you look up one row.

Two tables spell it differently: in therapy and therapyGroup the id column is key, and the JSON object is in value.

items.title: The data column holds everything else
items.text:
Most tables also have a data column: the row's complete JSON object as a string. The typed columns are a fast subset of it. Anything without a typed column is still in data, and ->> reaches into it with a JSON path:

-- The alternate base and the gnomAD-style id of the first five alleles; neither has a typed column
SELECT id,
       name,
       data->>'$.state.sequence' AS alt,
       [e.value FOR e IN CAST(data->'$.expressions' AS STRUCT(syntax VARCHAR, value VARCHAR)[])
                IF e.syntax = 'gnomad'][1] AS gnomad
FROM 'allele.parquet'
LIMIT 5;

id                                         name                         alt  gnomad
ga4gh:VA.KqJix9Wg3wCbUTjTt8CLY4TXToP2NyoC  NC_000016.10:g.376236G>A     A    16-376236-G-A
ga4gh:VA.B4RiRl78A-gSU0a3yOz_aLl2jR7qxpdW  NC_000002.12:g.107882735G>A  A    2-107882735-G-A
ga4gh:VA.E8L_Ltq8nC8OPjbEk1jasgkF9SXDKEkf  NC_000017.11:g.8173472G>A    A    17-8173472-G-A
…

->> returns text, and -> returns JSON that you can CAST to a typed list or struct, as expressions is here. In therapy and therapyGroup the same JSON is in value. Before 1.1.0, condition had no data column.

items.title: Reading a STRUCT column
items.text:
The most common first mistake is to treat a STRUCT column as text. In scv.parquet, classification is a whole record (a GA4GH MappableConcept), not a string:

SELECT count(*) FROM 'scv.parquet' WHERE classification = 'Pathogenic';

Conversion Error: Type VARCHAR with value 'Pathogenic' can't be cast to the destination type
STRUCT("type" VARCHAR, conceptType VARCHAR, "name" VARCHAR, primaryCoding STRUCT(code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR), …)

Name the field you want with a dot:

SELECT id,
       classification.name                AS classification,   -- what the submitter wrote
       classification.primaryCoding.code  AS code,             -- the normalized value
       quality.name                       AS submission_level
FROM 'scv.parquet'
LIMIT 5;

The same goes for strength, quality, and condition.primaryCoding:

SELECT id, name, primaryCoding.code AS medgen_cui, aliases[1] AS first_alias, len(aliases) AS n_aliases
FROM 'condition.parquet'
WHERE name = 'Marfan syndrome';

id                  name             medgen_cui  first_alias                   n_aliases
clinvar.trait:2645  Marfan syndrome  C0024796    FBN1-Related Marfan Syndrome  5

items.title: Never SELECT * on a big table
items.text:
This is the one warning on this page that costs real time if ignored. Parquet stores each column separately and compressed. A query reads only the columns it names, so naming fewer columns means reading less. SELECT * names them all, and on a big table "all" is mostly the data column.

Here is scv.parquet in the 2026-10-18 release, by column:

Column On disk In memory (uncompressed) data 2.10 GB 15.71 GB description 0.42 GB 2.21 GB extensions 0.39 GB 1.64 GB classification 0.12 GB 0.92 GB id 0.06 GB 0.25 GB everything else 0.13 GB 0.30 GB whole table 3.21 GB 21.0 GB

A 3 GB file becomes about 21 GB once decompressed, three quarters of it the data column. SELECT * FROM 'scv.parquet', or loading it whole into pandas, asks for all of it. On a laptop the machine swaps until it is unusable or the process is killed; in the browser console the tab runs out of memory.

The fix is always the same: name the columns you need, and leave data out unless you need something only it holds. The sizes of every table are in the column reference.

items.title: A worked example: what do submitters say?
items.text:
Count every SCV by its classification. The query reads only the classification fields (well under 1 MB on disk) instead of the whole 3 GB file, so it finishes in a fraction of a second on downloaded files. Over the network it needs a request per row group, which trips the console's rate limit, so run this one locally.

SELECT classification.name AS classification, count(*) AS n
FROM 'scv.parquet'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY n DESC;

It returns 44 distinct values, and some of them are the same call written differently:

classification            n
Uncertain significance    3,293,960
Likely benign             1,881,719
Benign                      648,029
Pathogenic                  517,828
Likely pathogenic           282,443
Uncertain Significance       32,593
…
pathogenic                    2,792
…
PATHOGENIC                       22

classification.name is the text the submitter sent, so case varies. Group by the normalized primaryCoding.code instead, and keep its system (the guideline the classification follows), because the same code can come from different guidelines:

SELECT classification.primaryCoding.code   AS code,
       classification.primaryCoding.system AS guideline,
       count(*) AS n
FROM 'scv.parquet'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY n DESC;

code                    guideline                                           n
uncertain significance  ACMG Guidelines, 2015                               3,326,410
likely benign           ACMG Guidelines, 2015                               1,902,052
benign                  ACMG Guidelines, 2015                                 651,462
pathogenic              ACMG Guidelines, 2015                                 520,642
likely pathogenic       ACMG Guidelines, 2015                                 290,567
not provided            ClinVar                                                29,121
…
tier 1                  AMP/ASCO/CAP (AAC) Guidelines, 2017                     1,018
likely oncogenic        ClinGen/CGC/VICC Guidelines for Oncogenicity, 2022        998
…

That collapses the 44 spellings into 34 code–guideline pairs. The normalization goes beyond case: the one SCV that says no known pathogenicity is counted under benign.

Next: the 22 tables and how they fit together, then joining them.

items.title: The 22 Tables
items.text:
Release

Counts and sizes on this page are from the 2026-10-18 release. They change with every release; the queries give you today's numbers.

The Parquet release is 22 tables, one per bundle section. They fall into six areas that you can learn one at a time. Variants and conditions are the nouns. Propositions say what is claimed about them. Statements say who claimed it, and how confidently.

The map renders at full size in a scrollable frame. Each area has a runnable query you can expand, and each table box links to that table's column reference below.

items.title: The six areas
items.text:
Area Tables The question it answers 1 · Variant variation, allele, copyNumberCount, copyNumberChange, location, sequenceReference, gene Which variant is this, and where is it on the genome? 2 · Condition & therapy condition, conditionSet, therapy, therapyGroup Which disease, tumor type or drug is the claim about? 3 · Proposition propositionPathogenicity, propositionClinvarCustom, propositionSomaticClinicalImpact, propositionOncogenicity What exactly is being claimed about the variant? 4 · SCV scv, evidenceLine, submitter What did each submitter say, how, and on what evidence? 5 · RCV rcv, rcv_evidenceLine What is ClinVar's combined call for this variant and this condition? 6 · VCV vcv, vcv_evidenceLine What is ClinVar's combined call for this variant across all its conditions?

Most questions start in area 1 or 2, go through area 3, and end in one statement area. The Joining Tables page covers each of those hops. For download links and the release layout, see Downloads → Parquet Files.

items.title: Ids tell you where to look
items.text:
Every row has an id, and the id's shape names its table. Learn these shapes before writing a join. Several columns can hold more than one kind of id, so the prefix tells you which table to join.

Id shape Example Table clinvar:<n> clinvar:51592 variation ga4gh:VA.<digest> ga4gh:VA.Apas_jvqBJU7l4DGHGlvTGRY3BBh-UR9 allele ga4gh:CN.<digest> ga4gh:CN.DRAu4AtQd-hge-7X3WhuN8ZP8Ly3tnZy copyNumberCount ga4gh:CX.<digest> ga4gh:CX.X1aEdg3zvDBvYfZfupzYACFNXKTi1Yh2 copyNumberChange ga4gh:SL.<digest> ga4gh:SL.PMlrYeTHc_PlcGkq_mRgtJ74aIZvjKCM location SQ.<digest> SQ.bN6Bx164NNk85Q4z_tOLZunW1BA-4vL_ sequenceReference ncbigene:<n> ncbigene:675 gene clinvar.trait:<n> clinvar.trait:9580 condition clinvar.traitset:<n> clinvar.traitset:10013 conditionSet (accessioned) clinvar.conditionset:vcv-<md5> clinvar.conditionset:vcv-50aae75c5e3a7740ab0c2f3ff9ebd970 conditionSet (minted) clinvar.therapy:<sha256> clinvar.therapy:b150cd67… therapy clinvar.therapygroup:<sha256> clinvar.therapygroup:3595163a… therapyGroup clinvar.submitter:<n> clinvar.submitter:500034 submitter clinvar.submission:SCV<n>.<ver> clinvar.submission:SCV000056982.2 scv — and evidenceLine, which shares the key SCV<n>-<CODE> SCV000056982-ASSOC a proposition table (a submission's proposition) VCV<n>-<G\|S>-<CODE>[-<LEVEL>] VCV000051592-G-PATH-CP a proposition table (an aggregate's proposition) VCV<n>.<ver>-<G\|S>-<CODE>[-<LEVEL>] VCV000051592.122-G-PATH-CP vcv RCV<n>.<ver>-<G\|S>-<CODE>[-<LEVEL>] RCV003486676.1-G-PATH-CP rcv <statement id>.contributing / .non-contributing VCV000051592.122-G-PATH-NOCP.contributing vcv_evidenceLine / rcv_evidenceLine

Two details are easy to miss:

  • A proposition id is its statement's id without the version. VCV000051592-G-PATH-CP is the proposition, and VCV000051592.122-G-PATH-CP is the statement about it.
  • A proposition id's classification code names its table. PATH is in propositionPathogenicity, ONCO in propositionOncogenicity, SCI, DIAG, PROG and TR in propositionSomaticClinicalImpact, and every other code in propositionClinvarCustom (see the code table under Reading a variant's statements). A query that spans several codes can read all four at once: the tables share one column schema, so read_parquet('proposition*.parquet') is a single table.

items.title: Where a traversal ends
items.text:
Five tables are leaves: they reference no other table, so a chain of joins stops there.

  • sequenceReference: the bottom of the variant chain (variation → allele → location → sequenceReference).
  • gene: reached from a variant's gene list.
  • condition: reached from a proposition, directly or through a conditionSet.
  • therapy: reached from a therapeutic-response proposition, directly or through a therapyGroup.
  • submitter: reached from an SCV's contributions.

scv is a leaf of the statement graph: RCV and VCV statements cite SCVs, but an SCV cites no other statement.

items.title: Reading a variant's statements
items.text:
A single variant usually has several VCV statements: one per classification type and aggregate level, in a germline lane and sometimes a somatic lane. The statement id encodes all three, as the diagram below shows. It also shows how somatic clinical-impact statements add an evidence-line layer, and which levels contribute to the aggregate call.

The same facts as text. A statement id reads <accession>.<version>-<lane>-<code>[-<level>], for example VCV000012871.94-G-PATH-CP.

Lane and classification code. The lane is G (germline) or S (somatic). The code is shorthand for the proposition type, and says which proposition table holds the proposition:

Lane Code Proposition type Proposition table Root statements G PATH VariantPathogenicityProposition propositionPathogenicity 4,434,756 G NP ClinvarNotProvidedProposition propositionClinvarCustom 27,921 G DR ClinvarDrugResponseProposition propositionClinvarCustom 2,760 G OTH ClinvarOtherProposition propositionClinvarCustom 2,171 G RF ClinvarRiskFactorProposition propositionClinvarCustom 1,072 G ASSOC ClinvarAssociationProposition propositionClinvarCustom 525 G AFF ClinvarAffectsProposition propositionClinvarCustom 331 G CDFS ClinvarConflictingDataFromSubmitterProposition propositionClinvarCustom 192 G PROTECT ClinvarProtectiveProposition propositionClinvarCustom 99 G CS ClinvarConfersSensitivityProposition propositionClinvarCustom 20 S ONCO VariantOncogenicityProposition propositionOncogenicity 1,905 S SCI VariantClinicalSignificanceProposition propositionSomaticClinicalImpact 1,317

Root statement counts are VCV roots. An SCV's proposition id uses the same codes without a lane (SCV000056982-ASSOC). Somatic clinical impact (SCI) also has evidence lines whose target_proposition_id names the specific impact: -TR (therapeutic response), -DIAG or -PROG, all in propositionSomaticClinicalImpact with the SCI propositions. Their tier is in evidenceOutcome: Level A/B is Tier I, Level C/D is Tier II.

Aggregate level. The level suffix matches the quality.name of the submissions it groups:

Level quality.name Precedence PG practice guidelines 5 EP expert panel 4 CP criteria provided 3 NOCP no assertion criteria provided 2 NOCL no classification 1 FLAG flagged set apart

A root statement takes its call from the highest level present, and the levels below it are marked non-contributing. Which level contributes therefore depends on the variant: a variant whose best submissions are NOCP contributes NOCP. Two exceptions: PG and EP both contribute when both are present (the practice guideline doesn't mask the expert panel), and flagged submissions never contribute.

items.title: The data column
items.text:
Almost every table has a data column holding the row's complete JSON object as a string, exactly as it appears in the JSON bundle. The typed columns are a convenient, fast subset of it. When a field has no typed column, reach into data:

SELECT id,
       data->>'$.contributions[0].contributor' AS first_contributor
FROM 'scv.parquet'
LIMIT 5;

Two things differ inside data. References are bundle pointers (#/submitter/clinvar.submitter:500034), whereas typed columns carry the bare id (clinvar.submitter:500034). And data is by far the largest column. Leave it out of your SELECT unless you need it; Working at Scale explains why.

Three tables break the pattern:

  • condition has camelCase columns (conceptType, primaryCoding), not snake_case. Its data column is new in 1.1.0; earlier releases don't have one.
  • therapy and therapyGroup name the id column key and hold the JSON object in value, not id and data. From 1.1.0 they also have typed columns (name, members, …). On earlier releases, read a therapy's name with value->>'name'.

items.title: Reading a table remotely
items.text:
Every table can be queried straight from https://data.clinvar-gkm.org/v1/1.1/parquet/<table>.parquet, without downloading it. How well that works depends on what you ask:

  • Cheap on any table: DESCRIBE, count(*), and LIMIT reads. These touch only the file's footer or its first chunk, so they return in under a second even on the 3.2 GB scv.parquet.
  • Fine on small tables: full scans of anything up to tens of megabytes (condition, gene, submitter, therapy, the somatic propositions).
  • Download first for big tables: a full scan or GROUP BY over scv, variation, propositionPathogenicity, or the aggregates reads every row group, one request each, in a burst. Remotely that takes tens of seconds and hundreds of megabytes, and a heavier query can still hit the CDN's limit of 250 requests per 10 seconds (HTTP 429). Download the table once and query it locally. See Working at Scale.

The sizes in the reference below tell you which category a table is in.

items.title: Column reference
items.text:
Every column of every table, from DESCRIBE on the 2026-10-18 release, with that release's row counts and file sizes (decimal units: 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes). Types are shown compactly: STRUCT(a, b) lists only the top-level fields, and [] marks a list. Expand Full nested types under a table for the complete DuckDB type, or run DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM '<table>.parquet' yourself.

Read a STRUCT field with a dot (classification.name) and a list with unnest(…) or an index (members[1]). Anatomy of a Table walks through both.

items.title: variation
items.text:
ClinVar's variants, one row per ClinVar Variation id, as Cat-VRS CategoricalVariant records. The subject of every proposition. Each row points at the concrete VRS variant(s) that define it.

variation.parquet · 4,691,827 rows · 3.9 GB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR clinvar:<variation id>, e.g. clinvar:51592. type VARCHAR Always CategoricalVariant. name VARCHAR ClinVar's preferred name, e.g. NM_000059.4(BRCA2):c.4090A>C (p.Ile1364Leu). extensions STRUCT(name, value_string, value_boolean, value_coding, value_hgvs_array, value_gene_array)[] Named ClinVar attributes, each {name, value_*} with the one value_* field matching its kind populated: clinvarVariationType, clinvarSubclassType, definingVrsVariationType, categoricalVariationType, clinvarCytogeneticLocation, clinvarHgvsList (→ value_hgvs_array; an entry's nucleotideExpression may carry extensions that keep ClinVar's submitted text when it wasn't valid HGVS: invalidClinvarExpression with expressionMerged, or originalClinvarExpression with expressionRepaired), clinvarGeneList (→ value_gene_array, whose .gene is a bare ncbigene:… id → gene.id), and VRS processing notes (vrsProcessingException, vrsPreProcessingIssue). mappings STRUCT(coding, relation)[] Identifiers for this variant in other systems: {coding{system, code, iris}, relation}. Always the ClinVar id (exactMatch); often dbSNP and ClinGen Allele Registry; sometimes dbVar, OMIM, UniProt, and locus-specific databases. members VARCHAR[] VRS ids of the concrete variants that are members of this category — ga4gh:VA. → allele, ga4gh:CN. → copyNumberCount, ga4gh:CX. → copyNumberChange. constraints STRUCT(type, allele, location, copies, copyChange, matchCharacteristic, relations)[] Cat-VRS constraints that define the category: DefiningAlleleConstraint (.allele), DefiningLocationConstraint (.location), CopyCountConstraint (.copies), CopyChangeConstraint (.copyChange); .relations lists allowed relations such as liftover_to, transcribed_to. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column. Full nested types — variation 
extensions  STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, value_string VARCHAR, value_boolean BOOLEAN, value_coding BIGINT, value_hgvs_array STRUCT(nucleotideExpression STRUCT(syntax VARCHAR, "value" VARCHAR, "extensions" STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, value_string VARCHAR, value_boolean BOOLEAN)[]), nucleotideType VARCHAR, maneSelect BOOLEAN, manePlus BOOLEAN, proteinExpression STRUCT(syntax VARCHAR, "value" VARCHAR), molecularConsequence STRUCT(code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, "name" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[])[])[], value_gene_array STRUCT(gene VARCHAR, relationship_type VARCHAR, "source" VARCHAR)[])[]
mappings  STRUCT(coding STRUCT("system" VARCHAR, code VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[]), relation VARCHAR)[]
constraints  STRUCT("type" VARCHAR, allele VARCHAR, "location" VARCHAR, copies BIGINT, copyChange VARCHAR, matchCharacteristic STRUCT("type" VARCHAR, primaryCoding STRUCT(code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[])), relations STRUCT("type" VARCHAR, primaryCoding STRUCT(code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[]))[])[]

items.title: allele
items.text:
VRS Allele records — a specific sequence change at a location. Reached from variation.members[] / constraints[].allele (ga4gh:VA. prefix).

allele.parquet · 4,598,672 rows · 1.1 GB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR ga4gh:VA.<digest> — the GA4GH computed identifier. type VARCHAR Always Allele. digest VARCHAR The digest part of the id (the id without ga4gh:VA.). name VARCHAR An HGVS expression for the allele, e.g. NC_000016.10:g.376236G>A. location_id VARCHAR ga4gh:SL.… → location.id. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: copyNumberCount
items.text:
VRS CopyNumberCount records — an absolute copy count over a region (ga4gh:CN. prefix).

copyNumberCount.parquet · 47,466 rows · 8.7 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR ga4gh:CN.<digest>. type VARCHAR Always CopyNumberCount. digest VARCHAR The digest part of the id. copies BIGINT The absolute copy number (0–7 in this release). location_id VARCHAR ga4gh:SL.… → location.id. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: copyNumberChange
items.text:
VRS CopyNumberChange records — a relative copy gain or loss over a region (ga4gh:CX. prefix).

copyNumberChange.parquet · 31,722 rows · 5.8 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR ga4gh:CX.<digest>. type VARCHAR Always CopyNumberChange. digest VARCHAR The digest part of the id. copy_change VARCHAR gain or loss. location_id VARCHAR ga4gh:SL.… → location.id. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: location
items.text:
VRS SequenceLocation records — a span on a reference sequence, shared by alleles and copy-number variants.

location.parquet · 4,215,441 rows · 714.9 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR ga4gh:SL.<digest>. type VARCHAR Always SequenceLocation. digest VARCHAR The digest part of the id. loc_start BIGINT Start coordinate (0-based, interbase). NULL when the start is an uncertain range — the range is in data as "start": [min, max]; use loc_start_min / loc_start_max instead. loc_end BIGINT End coordinate (interbase). NULL when the end is an uncertain range; use loc_end_min / loc_end_max instead. sequence_reference_id VARCHAR SQ.… → sequenceReference.id. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column. loc_start_min BIGINT Lower bound of the start. Equals loc_start for a definite start. For an uncertain range it is the range's min, or NULL when the range is open ([null, max], unbounded below). From 1.1.0. loc_start_max BIGINT Upper bound of the start. Equals loc_start for a definite start, otherwise the range's max. Never NULL. From 1.1.0. loc_end_min BIGINT Lower bound of the end. Equals loc_end for a definite end, otherwise the range's min. Never NULL. From 1.1.0. loc_end_max BIGINT Upper bound of the end. Equals loc_end for a definite end. For an uncertain range it is the range's max, or NULL when the range is open ([min, null], unbounded above). From 1.1.0.

loc_start_max and loc_end_min bound the span the variant certainly covers, and are set on every row, so window queries can use them without skipping uncertain-range locations (71,973 rows in 2026-10-18, all of them copy-number variant locations). loc_start_min and loc_end_max bound the widest span it may cover.

Why loc_start and loc_end, not start and end

In the bundle and in data, these fields are VRS's start and end. The typed columns carry a loc_ prefix because END is a reserved word in SQL. DuckDB and BigQuery both reject an unquoted end (SELECT end FROM … is a syntax error), so a column named end would have to be quoted as "end" or `end` in every query. start is not reserved, but it shares the prefix so the pair stays consistent, as do the four range-bound columns.

items.title: sequenceReference
items.text:
The reference sequences locations are placed on — RefSeq chromosomes, transcripts, and other sequences, keyed by their GA4GH refget id. A leaf: it references nothing.

sequenceReference.parquet · 214 rows · 28.9 KB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR SQ.<digest> — the refget accession (note: no ga4gh: prefix). type VARCHAR Always SequenceReference. refget_accession VARCHAR Same value as id. name VARCHAR The RefSeq accession, e.g. NC_000017.11, NM_000059.4. molecule_type VARCHAR genomic, mRNA, or RNA. residue_alphabet VARCHAR na (nucleic acid). data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: gene
items.text:
Genes referenced by variants' gene lists and by propositions' gene_context_id, keyed by NCBI Gene id. A leaf.

gene.parquet · 92,989 rows · 5.4 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR ncbigene:<n>, e.g. ncbigene:675 (BRCA2). concept_type VARCHAR Always gene. name VARCHAR The gene symbol, e.g. BRCA2. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string; adds primaryCoding (the NCBI Gene coding).

items.title: condition
items.text:
ClinVar's conditions (traits) — diseases, phenotypes, findings — one row per ClinVar trait. The object of most propositions. A leaf. camelCase column names (conceptType, primaryCoding), unlike the other tables.

condition.parquet · 23,414 rows · 4.7 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR clinvar.trait:<n>, e.g. clinvar.trait:9580. type VARCHAR Always MappableConcept. conceptType VARCHAR Disease, Phenotype, Trait, or Condition. name VARCHAR Preferred name, e.g. Hereditary spastic paraplegia 48. aliases VARCHAR[] Alternate names. primaryCoding STRUCT(name, code, system, iris) The MedGen coding: {name, code, system, iris}; primaryCoding.code is the MedGen CUI (e.g. C3150901). mappings STRUCT(coding, relation)[] Cross-references {coding{name, code, system, iris}, relation} — MONDO, Orphanet, OMIM, HPO, and others. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column. New in 1.1.0. Full nested types — condition 
primaryCoding  STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[])
mappings  STRUCT(coding STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, code VARCHAR, "system" VARCHAR, iris VARCHAR[]), relation VARCHAR)[]

items.title: conditionSet
items.text:
Sets of conditions a single proposition is about. Two kinds of row share the table: accessioned ClinVar TraitSets (clinvar.traitset:) and sets minted for VCV-level aggregates (clinvar.conditionset:vcv-…).

conditionSet.parquet · 100,706 rows · 11.0 MB

Column Type Description id VARCHAR clinvar.traitset:<n> (accessioned) or clinvar.conditionset:vcv-<md5> (minted). type VARCHAR Always ConceptSet. conceptSetType VARCHAR For TraitSets, ClinVar's set type — Disease, Finding, TraitChoice, DrugResponse. NULL on minted sets. membershipOperator VARCHAR AND (all members together) or OR (any member). Minted sets are OR. concepts VARCHAR[] Member ids, not names — clinvar.trait: ids, and on minted sets possibly a nested clinvar.traitset:. Re-join to condition (see Joining → Seam B). data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: therapy
items.text:
Drug therapies named by therapeutic-response propositions. A leaf. The id column is key, not id, and the JSON object is in value, not data.

therapy.parquet · 38 rows · 4.8 KB

Column Type Description key VARCHAR The therapy id, clinvar.therapy:<sha256> (content-addressed). value VARCHAR The JSON object as a string: {conceptType: "Drug", name, type}. name VARCHAR The therapy name. New in 1.1.0; on earlier releases use value->>'name'. concept_type VARCHAR Always Drug. New in 1.1.0.

items.title: therapyGroup
items.text:
Combination therapies — a set of therapy members. Same key/value shape as therapy, plus typed columns for the operator and members.

therapyGroup.parquet · 10 rows · 8.0 KB

Column Type Description key VARCHAR The group id, clinvar.therapygroup:<sha256>. value VARCHAR The JSON object as a string: {type, membershipOperator, concepts}, where concepts is a list of #/therapy/clinvar.therapy:… pointers. membership_operator VARCHAR Always AND: the members are given together. New in 1.1.0. members VARCHAR[] Member ids, clinvar.therapy:… → therapy.key. New in 1.1.0; on earlier releases the members are only in value.

items.title: 3 · Proposition
items.text:
From 1.1.0 propositions are grouped by meaning, in four tables that share one column schema. A proposition's table depends only on its type, and read_parquet('proposition*.parquet') reads all four as one table with no renaming. Before 1.1.0 they were grouped by the shape of their object, in varcond-, varcustom-, vartumor- and vartherapy-proposition; see Migrating from 1.0.

Table Proposition types (id codes) Rows Size propositionPathogenicity VariantPathogenicityProposition (PATH) 27,868,969 1.5 GB propositionClinvarCustom the 9 Clinvar* types and ClinvarUndefinedProposition (NP, DR, OTH, RF, ASSOC, AFF, CDFS, PROTECT, CS, UNDEF) 186,184 10.4 MB propositionSomaticClinicalImpact VariantClinicalSignificanceProposition (SCI), VariantDiagnosticProposition (DIAG), VariantPrognosticProposition (PROG), VariantTherapeuticResponseProposition (TR) 12,607 738.0 KB propositionOncogenicity VariantOncogenicityProposition (ONCO) 9,595 457.3 KB

items.title: The shared columns
items.text:
Every proposition table has exactly these columns, in this order. A column that does not apply to a row is NULL (submitted_gene_symbols: an empty list). Every column is derived from the bundle record in data.

Column Type Description id VARCHAR SCV<n>-<CODE> for a submission's proposition; VCV<n>-<G|S>-<CODE>[-<LEVEL>] or RCV… for an aggregate's — e.g. VCV000051592-G-PATH-CP. Matches the proposition_id of at most one statement. Ids did not change in 1.1.0. type VARCHAR The proposition class, e.g. VariantPathogenicityProposition, ClinvarRiskFactorProposition. predicate VARCHAR The relation, e.g. isCausalFor, isRiskFactorFor, hasClinicalSignificanceFor, predictsSensitivityTo. subject_variant_id VARCHAR clinvar:<n> → variation.id. object_id VARCHAR The object's id. Dispatch on object_type: a condition → condition.id, a conditionSet → conditionSet.id (accessioned clinvar.traitset: or minted clinvar.conditionset:), a therapy → therapy.key, a therapyGroup → therapyGroup.key. object_type VARCHAR The table object_id points at: condition, conditionSet, therapy or therapyGroup. Only Therapeutic Response propositions have a therapy object. condition_qualifier_id VARCHAR Therapeutic Response only: the tumor/condition context, clinvar.trait: → condition.id (13 rows). NULL elsewhere. gene_context_id VARCHAR ncbigene:<n> → gene.id: the gene-context qualifier's own NCBI Gene coding. NULL when there is no qualifier, and for the placeholder. SCV propositions only; see Gene context. gene_context_name VARCHAR Symbol of the proposition's gene-context gene (e.g. EGFR), or NULL. SCV propositions only. One representative gene per variant, not the submitter's genes. For the placeholder (gene_context_source = submittedNotNormalized) it is the submitter's symbol; releases before 1.1.0 hold the literal submitted genes were not normalized. A symbol, not an id: join on gene_context_id. submitted_gene_symbols VARCHAR[] The gene symbols the submitter gave, verbatim and in order (e.g. [MYCN, MYCNOS]). Empty when there are none. gene_context_source VARCHAR Where the gene-context gene came from: submittedSymbolMatches, submittedSymbolDiffers, inferredFromVariant or submittedNotNormalized. NULL on VCV and RCV propositions, and where there is no qualifier. mode_of_inheritance VARCHAR Mode-of-inheritance qualifier (e.g. Autosomal dominant inheritance), or NULL. Germline SCV propositions only. penetrance VARCHAR Penetrance qualifier, or NULL. Germline SCV propositions only. data VARCHAR Full JSON object as a string — see The data column.

items.title: propositionPathogenicity
items.text:
Germline pathogenicity claims (VariantPathogenicityProposition, predicate isCausalFor) at every level. By far the largest table. object_type is condition or conditionSet (2,951,614 rows, mostly VCV propositions over several conditions). 6,771,946 SCV rows carry a gene-context qualifier.

propositionPathogenicity.parquet · 27,868,969 rows · 1.5 GB

items.title: propositionClinvarCustom
items.text:
ClinVar's non-pathogenicity germline classifications, which have no standard VA-Spec proposition: not provided, drug response, risk factor, association, affects, protective, confers sensitivity, other, conflicting data from submitters, plus ClinvarUndefinedProposition, the fallback for a classification that maps to no defined type (no rows so far). object_type is condition or conditionSet.

propositionClinvarCustom.parquet · 186,184 rows · 10.4 MB

items.title: propositionSomaticClinicalImpact
items.text:
Somatic clinical impact: the clinical significance (SCI) that SCV, VCV and RCV statements classify, and the diagnostic (DIAG), prognostic (PROG) and therapeutic-response (TR) propositions that SCI evidence lines target. No statement classifies a DIAG, PROG or TR proposition directly; they are reached through evidenceLine.target_proposition_id. The 13 TR rows have a therapy or therapyGroup object and a condition_qualifier_id; every other row's object is a condition or conditionSet.

propositionSomaticClinicalImpact.parquet · 12,607 rows · 738.0 KB

items.title: propositionOncogenicity
items.text:
Somatic oncogenicity claims (VariantOncogenicityProposition, predicate isOncogenicFor). The object is the tumor type: almost always a condition, but 12 rows name a minted conditionSet.

propositionOncogenicity.parquet · 9,595 rows · 457.3 KB

items.title: Migrating from 1.0
items.text:
The ids, the records and the data column are unchanged; only the table a proposition is in, and some column names, changed in 1.1.0.

Proposition type (code) Before 1.1.0 From 1.1.0 VariantPathogenicityProposition (PATH) varcond-proposition propositionPathogenicity VariantClinicalSignificanceProposition (SCI), VariantDiagnosticProposition (DIAG), VariantPrognosticProposition (PROG) varcond-proposition propositionSomaticClinicalImpact VariantTherapeuticResponseProposition (TR) vartherapy-proposition propositionSomaticClinicalImpact VariantOncogenicityProposition (ONCO) vartumor-proposition propositionOncogenicity the Clinvar* types varcustom-proposition propositionClinvarCustom

Renamed columns: varcond-proposition.object_condition_id, vartumor-proposition.object_tumor_type_id and vartherapy-proposition.object_therapy are all object_id; varcustom-proposition.subject_id is subject_variant_id. New on every table: object_type, and the columns that only some of the old tables had (condition_qualifier_id, mode_of_inheritance, penetrance, the gene-context columns).

items.title: Gene context
items.text:
